title: Composing MIDI Tricks
intro: Getting ideas out of your head and into the sequencer before they evaporate. These tricks are about speed of capture first and correctness second — you can always fix it later, but you cannot un‑forget an idea.

tips.t: Capture the last thing you played, even when not recording
tips.d: If you played something great while the transport was rolling but not recording, hit ⇧R and Logic writes it to a region retroactively. MIDI works on any recent version, whether the project is playing or stopped. Audio needs Logic 11.2 or later: make sure the audio track is in focus and the transport is playing — Logic captures only while there is an incoming signal, needs at least four seconds of playback, and can save up to one minute of audio.

tips.t: Use the Step Input Keyboard for parts you cannot play
tips.d: Window > Show Step Input Keyboard. Enter notes one at a time at an exact rhythmic value. Complex parts get entered accurately without a single quantise pass.

tips.t: Draw notes with the Pencil, delete with the Eraser
tips.d: The Pencil creates a note whose length, velocity and MIDI channel match the last note you created or edited. To remove a note, select it and press Delete, or click it with the Eraser tool. ⌥-drag a note to copy it to a new position.

tips.t: Use the Chord Trigger MIDI plugin to play chords with one finger
tips.d: Insert Chord Trigger in the MIDI FX slot and click Learn. Click the trigger key you want on the upper keyboard first, then click the notes of the chord on the lower keyboard, then click Learn again to finish. Whole progressions become one-finger performances.

tips.t: Force everything into key with Transposer's scale quantize
tips.d: Insert the Transposer MIDI FX and set its Root and Scale pop-up menus. Transposer transposes incoming MIDI notes in real time and corrects them to the selected scale, so every wrong note you play is pulled to the nearest right one as you play. Pick User and switch notes off on the on-screen keyboard to build your own scale.

tips.t: Use Arpeggiator to generate parts, then commit them
tips.d: Insert Arpeggiator and dial in a pattern, then commit it with Bounce in Place: Logic renders the selected region — including every active plug-in and its automation — to a 24-bit audio file at the project sample rate, so the live effect becomes a fixed part you can edit as audio.
Select a region and use the Region inspector's Transpose field. It is non‑destructive, so you can audition a key change for the whole song in seconds.

tips.t: Use the Modifier MIDI plugin to remap anything to anything
tips.d: The Modifier MIDI plug-in reassigns or filters a single continuous controller or fader event. Pick the incoming type in Input Event and the outgoing type in Re-Assign To — modwheel into aftertouch, pitchbend into expression — and use the Scale and Add sliders to rescale or offset the values on the way out.

groups.heading: Working fast while ideas are hot

tips.t: Merge takes when you are layering, not replacing
tips.d: For building up a drum pattern one element per pass, set MIDI cycle recording to Merge instead. Each loop adds to the same region.

tips.t: Freeze the instrument as soon as the part is done
tips.d: Click the Freeze button in the track header to render the software instrument to audio. Your CPU comes back and the part is locked in.

tips.t: Drag a MIDI region onto an audio track to bounce it instantly
tips.d: Select the MIDI region and use Bounce in Place. Logic renders it through the instrument and every active plug-in, plus automation, to a 24-bit audio region at the project sample rate. It is the fastest way to commit an idea to audio.

tips.t: Keep one “sketch” instrument track loaded at all times
tips.d: A piano patch on a permanently armed track means any idea is three seconds from being captured. The moment capture takes effort, ideas stop arriving.

tips.t: Use Note Repeat for hi‑hats and rolls
tips.d: In Step Sequencer, choose Note Repeat from the Edit Mode selector, then drag up on a hi-hat step to slice it into more repeats (1 to 16) or down for fewer. The inspector adds velocity ramp, velocity curve and Distribution for each step, so a roll can accelerate or decelerate instead of sitting flat.
